usage: Said to others, never about your own plate
examples: Bare minimum a server says setting down a plate
이거 제가 직접 만들었어요. 맛있게 드세요.
I made this myself. Enjoy your meal.
Host adds 직접 (in person) to show effort
주문하신 음식 다 나왔습니다. 맛있게 드세요.
All your dishes are out. Please enjoy.
Real restaurant line; 나왔습니다 = the food has come out
nuance: 맛있게 드세요 literally stacks 맛있게 'deliciously' + 드세요, the honorific imperative of 들다/먹다 'to eat', so it means 'please eat (this) deliciously' — an invitation aimed at the other person, never a comment on your own food. The dividing line from plain 드세요 ('please eat') is the adverb 맛있게: it adds the warm wish that the food taste good, the way English 'enjoy your meal' adds feeling to 'eat'. 드세요 is the polite honorific of 먹어요; you use 드세요 to guests, customers and elders, but 먹어 to a child or close friend. It collocates with 많이 (a lot), 천천히 (slowly), 따뜻할 때 (while it's warm). English speakers wrongly say it about themselves before digging in — but you can't wish yourself a good meal; if you're the one eating, say 잘 먹겠습니다 instead.

The phrase is a wish directed at others; you cannot tell yourself to enjoy. Say 잘 먹겠습니다 ('I will eat well') to your host instead.

먹다 is the plain verb; to someone you respect the honorific 들다 is expected, so 드세요, not 먹으세요, sounds properly polite.

english: I look forward to working with you
usage: Please take good care of it / me
I look forward to working with you
Please treat me well going forward
examples: I look forward to working with you.
On its own, ending a first greeting
오늘부터 같이 일하게 됐어요. 잘 부탁드려요.
I start working with you today. Please treat me kindly.
New coworker; 게 됐어요 = it came to be
Please take good care of my child.
Parent to teacher; 드리겠습니다 is the humblest level
nuance: 부탁 is Sino-Korean 付託 'to entrust/commit (a request) to someone', and 드리다 is the humble 'to give (upward to a superior)', so 부탁드려요 literally means 'I humbly hand you my request' — far more deferential than plain 부탁해요. Add 잘 ('well') and it becomes the all-purpose Korean phrase for 'please look after this/me kindly', said at first meetings, when joining a team, or when entrusting any task. It has no clean English equivalent: depending on context it covers 'nice to meet you', 'I look forward to working with you', and 'please take care of it'. The near-synonym 도와주세요 ('please help me') is a concrete request for assistance, while 잘 부탁드려요 is a softer, relationship-building bow that asks for general goodwill, not a specific action. English speakers misread it as a literal plea for help and look for what task to do; really it is social glue, so you simply receive it warmly. Never answer a polite 부탁드려요 with the casual 부탁해 back to a senior.

examples: Quick shout when someone's about to trip
The floor's slippery, so be careful.
It's late, so get home safe.
nuance: 조심하세요 is built on Sino-Korean 操心 ('to manage/hold the heart-mind'), literally 'keep your mind on guard', and the 하다 verb takes the honorific imperative 하세요, so it means 'please be careful'. It works both as a genuine safety warning and, very commonly, as a caring farewell, so it overlaps with 잘 가세요 but adds the nuance of 'mind yourself'. A signature pattern is NOUN + 조심하세요, where the noun names the danger: 발 조심 (your feet), 계단 조심 (the stairs), 감기 조심 (catching cold), 차 조심 (cars). English speakers wrongly tack on 조심 with the object particle as 발을 조심하세요 — natural Korean usually drops the particle here, just 발 조심하세요. Drop the honorific to 조심해 only with close friends or juniors.

usage: 잘 makes it humbler, not 'know well'
examples: I don't know what this word means.
I still don't know when it'll finish.
nuance: 모르다 is the standalone verb 'to not know' (the opposite of 알다 'to know'), and 모르겠어요 adds -겠- before the polite 어요 ending. That -겠- is not future tense here; it softens the assertion into 'I'm not sure / I can't seem to tell', so 모르겠어요 sounds more tentative and humble than the flat 몰라요. The contrast matters: 몰라요 is a blunt fact ('I don't know'), even slightly curt or dismissive, while 모르겠어요 hedges politely and is what you'd say to a customer, teacher, or stranger. Adding 잘 in front (잘 모르겠어요) does NOT mean 'I know well' — counterintuitively it intensifies the not-knowing into 'I really have no idea', a common trap for English speakers who read 잘 as 'well'. It frequently embeds a question with -ㄴ지/-ㄹ지: 어디인지 모르겠어요 (I don't know where), 맞는지 모르겠어요 (I'm not sure if it's right). Because Korean rarely uses subject pronouns, you usually drop 저는 and just say 모르겠어요.

examples: One sec, let me grab this call.
Excuse me, let me get past.
Polite way through a packed subway
nuance: 잠깐 means 'a brief moment, a short while', 만 is the particle 'only/just', and the 요 makes it polite — so 잠깐만요 is literally 'just a brief moment, please', i.e. 'hold on a sec'. It does double duty: asking someone to wait, and politely getting their attention or asking them to make way, much like English 'excuse me' / 'one second'. Its near-twin 잠시만요 is essentially the same but a touch more formal and softer-sounding (잠시 is the more literary word for 'a moment'), so you'd lean to 잠시만요 with customers or in announcements, 잠깐만요 in everyday speech. It contrasts with 기다려요 ('wait'), which is a direct command to wait; 잠깐만요 is gentler because 만 frames it as 'only a tiny bit'. English speakers often over-formalize and say 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 every time, but in fast daily life the clipped 잠깐만요 is what natives actually use. Drop the 요 to 잠깐만 only with friends.

Using 잠깐만요 to make someone wait a long time.
It promises only a tiny pause (만 = just); for a real wait, say 조금만 기다려 주세요 or give a time, or it feels misleading.

nuance: 천만에요 comes from 천만 (Sino-Korean 千萬 'ten million') + 에요, an idiom meaning roughly 'not in ten million (ways)' — i.e. 'don't even think of it', hence 'you're welcome / not at all'. It is the textbook reply to 감사합니다, but in real life it sounds a bit formal and even slightly old-fashioned, so younger Koreans more often deflect with 아니에요 ('no, no'), 별말씀을요, or a casual 뭘요. Compare the registers: 아니에요 is the everyday warm 'oh it was nothing', 별말씀을요 is humbly brushing off thanks or praise, and 천만에요 is the dictionary-perfect but stiffer 'you're welcome'. English speakers, mapping 'you're welcome' one-to-one, overuse 천만에요 and can sound textbook-ish; among friends a simple 응 or 아니야 fits better. Note 천만에요 only answers thanks, whereas 별말씀을요 also deflects compliments, so they aren't fully interchangeable. Keep the 요 ending; 천만에 alone is rarely said.

usage: Humble reply to thanks or praise
examples: Quiet, humble deflection on its own
It went well thanks to you. — Don't mention it.
You're so kind. — Oh, you flatter me.
Here it deflects praise, not thanks
nuance: 별말씀을요 breaks down as 별 ('special, out of the ordinary', Sino-Korean 別) + 말씀 (the humble/honorific word for 'words, what you say') + 을 (object particle) + 요, literally 'such special words (you say)!' — an idiom that humbly waves away thanks or praise, like English 'don't mention it' or 'you flatter me'. Its register is courteous and a touch humble, common among adults in polite exchanges; it's softer and more self-effacing than the brisk dictionary reply 천만에요. The key distinction from 천만에요 is range: 천만에요 only answers 감사합니다, but 별말씀을요 also deflects compliments ('you're too kind'), because you're literally protesting the 'special words' someone offered. The full form 별말씀을 다 하세요 ('you say all sorts of flattering things') leans even more into brushing off praise. English speakers stumble on the spelling and pronunciation — it's 말씀 (honorific) not 말 — and on the liaison, where 을요 links into [으료]. Don't reduce it to 별말 (that means 'a strange remark'), and keep 말씀, the respectful form.

usage: Get home safe and come again
examples: Cheery shout as you leave a shop
Did you enjoy it? Please come again.
nuance: 다음에 ('next time', 다음 'next' + 에 'at') + 또 ('again') + 오세요 (honorific imperative of 오다 'to come') = 'please come again next time' — the warm send-off shop and restaurant staff give customers. Note the difference from 다음에 봐요 ('see you next time'), which is a casual mutual goodbye between friends, whereas 다음에 또 오세요 flows one way, host inviting guest back. The little word 또 is doing the 'again' work; 다시 also means 'again' but leans toward 'redo/once more', while 또 fits 'come back another time'. The big pitfall for English speakers is using it the wrong direction: customers almost never say it back — you simply reply 네, 감사합니다 or 잘 먹었습니다. Only the one staying behind (the host) issues the invitation to return.

usage: Here it is / here you go
examples: Said while passing an item across
nuance: 여기 있어요 = 여기 ('here', this place) + 있어요, the polite form of 있다 'to exist / to be (located)', so literally 'it is here' — used the moment you physically hand something over, like English 'here you go / here it is'. 있다 is the existence-and-location verb (the opposite of 없다 'to not exist'); don't confuse it with 이다 'to be (X)', so 'here it is' is 여기 있어요, never 여기 이에요. The fuller, more formal 여기 있습니다 is what polished service staff say. Near-synonym 여기 있어요 vs 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you'): the latter announces the giving, while 여기 있어요 presents the thing as already in hand. English speakers sometimes use 여기요 trying to say 'here you go' when handing an item — but bare 여기요 reads as 'excuse me, server', so add 있어요 when you mean 'here it is'.

있다 has its own antonym 없다; 'it's not here' is 여기 없어요, not 안 있어요.

usage: How much time does it take?
examples: -까지 = up to/as far as the airport
nuance: 얼마나 걸려요? combines 얼마나 ('how much / to what extent') with 걸리다 'to take (time), to be required', in the polite form 걸려요 — so it asks 'how much (time) does it take?'. The headword 걸리다 here means 'to take time'; the same verb also means 'to be caught/hung' or 'to catch (an illness)', so context disambiguates (시간이 걸리다 = takes time vs 감기에 걸리다 = catch a cold). The big trap for English speakers is mixing it up with 얼마예요? — that asks PRICE ('how much is it?'), while 얼마나 걸려요? asks DURATION; the extra 나 and the verb 걸리다 are what flip 'how much money' into 'how much time'. You sharpen the question with front modifiers: a destination with -까지 (집까지 'to home'), a means with -로 (지하철로 'by subway', 걸어서 'on foot'), or a start point with -에서/서 (여기서 'from here'). Korean puts the time word 시간이 optionally before 걸려요; you can drop it because 걸리다 already implies time. Answer with a duration like 30분쯤 걸려요 ('about 30 minutes').

mistakes: Asking 얼마예요? when you mean 'how long does it take?'
얼마예요? asks the price; duration needs the verb 걸리다 → 얼마나 걸려요? Mixing them gets you a cost, not a time.
Marking the destination with -에 instead of -까지.
For 'how long TO a place', the goal-of-extent particle is -까지: 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요? -에 marks a static location, not the endpoint of travel time.
Saying 얼마나 시간 걸려요 with no particle on 시간.
If you state the time noun, mark it as subject: 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? Or just drop 시간 entirely — 얼마나 걸려요? already means 'how long'.

examples: 이 + noun directly; pointing at a machine
nuance: 이거 뭐예요? = 이거 (the casual spoken contraction of 이것 'this thing') + 뭐 (the colloquial form of 무엇 'what') + 예요 (polite copula) — the everyday 'what is this?' you say while pointing. Three contraction layers trip up learners: 이것 → 이거 in speech; 이것이 (with subject particle) → 이게; and 무엇이에요 → 뭐예요. So 이거 뭐예요? and 이게 뭐예요? are both fine, the second just adds the subject marker and sounds a touch more careful. The distance set is 이거 (this, near me) / 그거 (that, near you) / 저거 (that, away from both) — pick by where the object is. The headword 뭐 is for THINGS; the crucial pitfall is using it for PEOPLE — 'who is this?' must be 누구예요?, never 뭐예요?, which would sound rude about a person. Also keep the copula attached: 뭐예요 fuses 뭐 + 이에요; writing 뭐 이에요 separately is unnatural. For an object's purpose rather than identity, switch to 이거 뭐 하는 거예요? ('what does this do?').

mistakes: Using 이거 뭐예요? about a person.
뭐 (what) is for things only; asking 'who is this?' takes 누구 → 이분 누구세요? Using 뭐예요 for a person is grammatically wrong and sounds rude.
Writing 이것이에요 / 무엇이에요 in casual speech.
Spoken Korean contracts these to 이게 / 뭐예요. The full forms are correct but sound stiff and written; natives say 이거 뭐예요?
Mixing up the distance words 이거/그거/저거.
이거 = near me, 그거 = near you, 저거 = away from both. Pointing at a far object but saying 이거 confuses the listener about which thing you mean.

usage: Polite heads-up about your own move
examples: Excusing yourself with a soft 좀
Excuse me, may I use the restroom?
Asking in a cafe; permission form
밥 먹기 전에 화장실 좀 다녀올게요.
I'll hit the restroom before we eat.
nuance: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 = 화장실 (Sino-Korean 化粧室, literally 'makeup/grooming room', the standard polite word for toilet) + 좀 (softener, a worn-down 조금 'a little') + 쓸게요, the -ㄹ게요 form of 쓰다 'to use'. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the key: it announces YOUR OWN intention/plan, as a courteous heads-up ('I'm going to use it, just letting you know'), not a request for permission. That separates it sharply from 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? ('may I use the restroom?'), which uses -아도 돼요 to actually ASK permission — say 쓸게요 in your own home or where it's obviously fine, but 써도 돼요? in someone's house or a shop where you need an OK. The little 좀 isn't 'a little' literally; it lubricates the sentence, making any request gentler. On vocabulary, 화장실 (the room) is the polite term, not the blunt 변소; and to ask its location it's 화장실 어디예요?. English speakers wrongly use the announcing 쓸게요 when they should be asking — if permission is in doubt, switch to 써도 돼요?. Also note 쓰다 'to use' is a separate verb from 쓰다 'to write', distinguished by context.

-ㄹ게요 announces your own plan, not a request. In someone's home or a shop, ask 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? with the permission ending -아도 돼요.
Treating 좀 as the literal 'a little'.
Here 좀 is a politeness softener that smooths the request, not a quantity. 화장실 좀 쓸게요 doesn't mean 'use the restroom a little'.
Calling the room 변소 or asking 화장실 있어요? to find it.
